name: ICS Scenario B2 — IEC-104 / Industroyer (Purdue + DMZ)
description: A Purdue-aligned Industroyer lab: Enterprise IT → Industrial DMZ → OT → Process, with two boundary firewalls, an SMBv1 file server, a DMZ file-transfer gateway, a historian that leaks a reused OT credential, a dual-homed IEC-104 RTU, an OVS SPAN to the IDS, and web UIs on the HMI and the substation projector. A more realistic rebuild of Scenario B — the attacker crosses the DMZ (iot → it-fileserver → gateway → historian → ew) before one legitimate IEC-104 command trips the breaker. Uses the tollan Docker Hub registry (you'll be prompted to add it). Ships the 'Industroyer across the Purdue model' tutorial; classroom guide is docs/ics-scenarios/scenario-b2-classroom-walkthrough.md.

topology.name: ICS Scenario B2 — IEC-104 / Industroyer (Purdue + DMZ)
topology.description: Four Purdue zones (IT 10.0.5.0/24 → DMZ 10.0.4.0/24 → OT 10.0.3.0/24 → PROCESS 10.0.1.0/24), two nftables firewalls (fw-it, fw-ot) flanking the DMZ, a dual-homed IEC-104 RTU, and an OVS SPAN to the IDS. Import after syncing the `tollan` registry. Node behaviour lives in the tollan images; design in docs/ics-scenarios/ics-scenario-b-industroyer-plan.md.

cells.source:
# Industroyer across the Purdue model

This walkthrough recreates the kind of attack behind the 2016 Ukraine power-grid incident, but on a **realistic, segmented plant** modelled on the **Purdue reference architecture**:

- **Enterprise IT** (`10.0.5.0/24`) — office machines.
- **Industrial DMZ** (`10.0.4.0/24`) — the only bridge between office and plant: a file-transfer **gateway** and a **historian**.
- **OT / Operations** (`10.0.3.0/24`) — the control network: HMI, engineering workstation, and the **RTU** that drives the breaker.
- **Process** (`10.0.1.0/24`) — Level 0: the physical feeder.

**There is no direct office→plant path.** Two firewalls (`fw-it`, `fw-ot`) flank the DMZ, and only two narrow flows are allowed. The attacker has to **hop the whole chain** — `iot → it-fileserver → gateway → historian → ew` — before a single legitimate IEC-104 command trips the breaker.

> **Keep two views open** as you go: select **`hmi`** → **Open web UI** (breaker state) and **`process-sim`** → **Open web UI** (the physical feeder: ENERGIZED/DARK, powered %, current, voltage). They turn red/dark when the breaker trips.
>
> Run with **Next step**, or one cell at a time with ▶. Each command is typed into the node's own terminal — so once a cell SSHes into the next host, the cells that follow run **there**.

## 1 · The segmented, monitored plant

First we arm the environment the way a real site would run it:

- **`fw-it`** permits exactly one IT→DMZ flow: `it-fileserver → gateway` (file transfer). Everything else office→plant is dropped.
- **`fw-ot`** permits exactly one DMZ→OT flow: the **historian**'s data feed into OT. (It's deliberately **over-broad** — more than a telemetry feed needs — which is the mistake the attacker will exploit.)
- The **IDS** (Zeek) starts watching the OT network over the switch's SPAN mirror.

Run the three setup cells.

cells.command:
nft insert rule inet filter forward ip saddr 10.0.4.30 ip daddr 10.0.3.0/24 accept
nft insert rule inet filter forward ip saddr 10.0.5.30 ip daddr 10.0.4.20 tcp dport 22 accept
echo 'FW-IT: it-fileserver -> gateway (SFTP) allowed; historian -> OT data feed allowed; all else office->plant dropped'
nft list chain inet filter forward

nft insert rule inet filter forward ip saddr 10.0.4.30 ip daddr 10.0.3.0/24 accept
echo 'FW-OT: historian -> OT allowed (over-broad: reaches the whole OT subnet, not just a telemetry port); every other DMZ->OT dropped'
nft list chain inet filter forward

mkdir -p /root/zeeklogs
nohup sh -c 'cd /root/zeeklogs && exec zeek -i eth0 -C' >/tmp/zeek.out 2>&1 &
sleep 2 && echo 'Zeek is now watching the OT network (SPAN mirror); logs in /root/zeeklogs'

cells.source:
## 2 · Normal operations

Open the **`hmi`** and **`process-sim`** web UIs now. The breaker is **CLOSED**, the feeder is **ENERGIZED** (100% · ~420 A · 11 kV). The operator controls the breaker from the HMI — click **Open** then **Close** on the HMI page and watch both views react. Ordinary, authorized control.

Now the attacker arrives.

## 3 · Foothold on the office network

The attacker has taken over an **IoT device** (`iot`) on the office LAN — a smart sensor/camera-class box with a shell. First question for any intruder: *where am I, and what else is on this network?*

The scan finds **`it-fileserver`** at `.30` (and the firewall at `.1`). But can the office reach the **plant** directly? Try the RTU's IEC-104 control port — the firewall **drops it** (office→plant is denied):

## 4 · Take the file server (SMBv1 + reused creds)

Filtered — segmentation is doing its job. So the attacker needs a way *around* it. The only office host the firewall lets into the DMZ is **`it-fileserver`**, so that's the stepping stone. It runs an **old, vulnerable Samba (4.5.9)** exposing an SMBv1 share and reuses the lab's weak password. List its shares over SMB with the reused credential, then take a shell on it the same way.

## 5 · Into the DMZ

This terminal is now a shell on **`it-fileserver`** — the one office host the firewall lets reach the DMZ **gateway** (over SFTP, the single permitted IT→DMZ flow). That transfer channel reuses the same password, so it's also a shell. Pivot in:

## 6 · Loot a credential from the historian

Now on the **`gateway`**, inside the DMZ. The gateway itself can't reach OT — but the **historian** can (its data feed). Move to the historian (intra-DMZ, no firewall), then read its data-collector config. Real sites leave secrets in config and backup files — here the collector stores a **reused OT service-account password**.

## 7 · Pivot into OT

The config hands over an OT credential and names the hosts it opens — including the **engineering workstation** (`ew`, `10.0.3.15`). From the gateway this would be blocked, but the **historian's over-broad OT rule** lets it through. Confirm the RTU is reachable from here, then SSH to the EW with the looted (reused) password.

## 8 · Reach the RTU

This shell is now on the **engineering workstation — inside OT, past both firewalls**. The RTU's IEC-104 control port is directly reachable here, and the breaker is CLOSED. The segmentation was never broken; the attacker went *around* it, one weak link at a time.

## 9 · Trip the breaker

The attacker sends the **same IEC-104 command an engineer would** — a single control command to the breaker — but from inside the plant, against the live feeder. On the wire it is identical to authorized control.

**Watch the HMI flip to OPEN · red and `process-sim` go DARK** (0% · 0 A · 0 kV). No operator did this.

## 10 · Recovery, then loss of control

The operator notices and **closes the breaker from the HMI** (click **Close** on the HMI page). It works — green again, feeder re-energized. Normal recovery… for now.

Then the attacker **denies recovery** with an injected loop on the EW: the instant the breaker is closed, it re-opens. **This cell runs until you press `Ctrl-C` in its terminal.**

cells.command: while sleep 1; do breaker open >/dev/null 2>&1; done

cells.source:
With the loop running, have the operator try again — **click Close on the HMI**. The breaker snaps straight back to **OPEN**. The operator has **lost control** of the feeder. This is the Industroyer effect.

When you've seen it, press **Ctrl-C** in this terminal to stop the loop.

## 11 · What the defender saw

On the **IDS**, the connection log shows the whole attack only as **plain TCP to port 2404** — this Zeek has no IEC-104 analyzer loaded, so it can't see *what* command was sent.

And the sharper point: even **with** an IEC-104 parser, the trip is a perfectly valid command — identical to what the HMI sends. What actually stands out is the **source**: the command came from the **engineering workstation**, a host that does not normally drive the RTU. Telling the attack apart needs **context** (*who* is talking to the RTU, *from where*), not just protocol decoding.

cells.command:
echo 'Connections seen to the RTU control port (2404):'
grep -v '^#' /root/zeeklogs/conn.log 2>/dev/null | awk '$6==2404 {print "  "$3" -> "$5":2404   proto="$7"   service="$8}' | tail

cells.source:
## Reset & recap

**Reset:** press `Ctrl-C` in the attacker's re-trip terminal, click **Close** on the HMI, then `exit` the shells back out to `iot`.

**What this taught:**
- **Defense in depth held, until it didn't.** Two firewalls and a DMZ blocked every *direct* path — but a **chain of weak links** (an SMBv1 file server, a reused password, an over-broad historian rule, a looted credential) let the attacker hop IT → DMZ → OT anyway.
- The final act used a **legitimate protocol command**. No exploit, no malware — just reachability plus an unauthenticated OT protocol.
- **Detection is hard**: even decoded, the command is valid — flagging it needs **context** (an unexpected source talking to the RTU), not just protocol awareness.

**Defenses:** least-privilege firewall rules (no over-broad DMZ→OT), no reused credentials / secret sprawl, retire SMBv1, and context-aware OT monitoring (baseline *which* hosts command the RTU).
